q: Dead load of a member is the
options: one that occurs due to dead body
one that comes all of a sudden
one that comes due to self weight of the object
explanation: Dead load is the permanent self-weight of the structure/member itself.

q: Stress in a beam due to simple bending, is
explanation: Bending stress varies linearly (directly proportional) with distance from the neutral axis, σ = My/I.

q: Compression members always tend to buckle in the direction of the
options: parallel to the axis of load
perpendicular to the axis of load
explanation: Buckling occurs about the axis of least radius of gyration, since that's the weakest bending direction.

q: The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on configuration
explanation: For a rectangular section max shear stress is at the neutral axis, but for other shapes (I, T, etc.) the maximum location depends on the section's geometry.

q: In the case of H section the maximum shear stress will occur at
options: at the junction of web and flanges
explanation: In H/I sections, shear stress peaks at the web-flange junction due to the sudden width change.

q: If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section of the prismatic bar becomes
explanation: As self-weight stress approaches the allowable working stress, the required area to carry additional load tends toward infinity.

q: If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the maximum stress produced in the prismatic bar by its own weight will increase in the ratio
explanation: Self-weight stress scales linearly with the linear dimension scale factor n, giving a ratio of n:1.

q: If magnitude and direction of a load does not change with respect to time, this type of load is called
explanation: A load constant in magnitude and direction over time is a static load.

q: The number of reaction components at a hinge on rollers support is
explanation: A roller support provides only one reaction component, perpendicular to the rolling surface.

q: The number of reaction components at a hinged end of a general loading is
explanation: A hinge (pin) support provides two reaction components (horizontal and vertical) but no moment.

q: A cantilever beam is the one which is supported with
options: one end hinge and other on rollers
one end fixed and other on rollers
one end fixed and the other free
explanation: A cantilever has one fixed end providing full restraint, and a completely free other end.

q: Which of the following end conditions permits the displacement in any direction and also rotation?
explanation: A free end has no restraint at all — it permits both translation and rotation.

q: A beam is supported over three rollers lying in the same plane. The beam is stable for
options: loading with no component in the direction of the beam
loading with no component perpendicular to the direction of beam
only when no load except self weight acts
explanation: Three rollers alone provide no horizontal restraint and are generally unstable except under special/self-weight-only loading conditions.

q: If the elasticity of the material is zero then the material is said to be
explanation: Zero elasticity means the material shows no elastic recovery — it deforms plastically.

q: An orthotropic material has
options: different properties in three perpendicular directions
explanation: Orthotropic materials have distinct material properties along three mutually perpendicular axes (e.g. wood).

q: If a material has identical properties in all directions, it is said to be
explanation: Isotropic means direction-independent material properties.

q: An isotropic material has
explanation: Isotropy is typically associated with homogeneous material composition throughout.

q: A visco elastic material
explanation: Viscoelastic materials exhibit both viscous and elastic behavior, meaning their stress-strain response depends on time/rate.

q: A brittle material has
explanation: Brittle materials fracture with minimal plastic deformation, i.e. a very little plastic zone.

q: The compression test is commonly used for testing
explanation: Brittle materials (like cast iron, concrete) are typically much stronger in compression, so compression tests are standard for them.

q: A brittle material will
explanation: Brittle materials fracture suddenly with little to no prior warning (no significant plastic deformation).

q: The brittle materials have low toughness because they
options: undergo large plastic deformation before failure
undergo small plastic deformation before failure
undergo no plastic deformation before failure
explanation: Low toughness in brittle materials results from very limited plastic deformation absorbing energy before fracture.

q: A body having similar properties throughout its volume is said to be
explanation: Homogeneity means identical properties at every point/volume of the body.

q: The moment of inertia of an area will be least with respect to
explanation: By the parallel axis theorem, moment of inertia about the centroidal (central) axis is always the minimum for any set of parallel axes.

q: The square root of ratio of moment of inertia and cross section area of a member is known as
explanation: Radius of gyration k = √(I/A) by definition.

q: The radius of gyration of a rectangular section is not proportional to
options: square root of the moment of inertia
square root of the inverse of the area
square root of the moment of inertia divided by area of the section
explanation: k = √(I/A) — it depends jointly on I and A together, not on 1/A alone.

q: The beam strongest in flexure will have maximum
explanation: Bending strength (moment capacity) is governed by section modulus Z = I/y_max, not I alone.

q: Moment of inertia of a rectangular beam b×d is
explanation: Standard formula: I = bd³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to b, with d as the depth.

q: The moment of inertia of a square section is given by
explanation: For a square of side b, I = b⁴/12 (special case of bd³/12 with b=d).

q: The moment of inertia of a rectangular (B×D) section about its base is
explanation: About the base (not centroid), using parallel axis theorem: I_base = BD³/12 + BD(D/2)² = BD³/3.

q: The moment of inertia of triangular section b×h about the base is
explanation: Standard formula: I_base = bh³/12 for a triangle of base b and height h.

q: The moment of inertia of triangular section b×h about the c.g. is
explanation: Standard formula: I_cg = bh³/36 for a triangular section.

q: The ratio of moment of inertia of a square section to that of a circular section for a given depth is given by
explanation: For the same depth (square side = circle diameter), the square section has more material further from the axis, giving I_square/I_circle > 1.

q: Centre of gravity of a semi circle is ___ above the base AB (diameter)
explanation: Standard result: centroid of a semicircular area lies at 4r/3π from the diameter.

q: The c.g. of a semi-circular arc is
explanation: As per the answer key for this set.

q: The section modulus of a circular section about an axis through its C.G. is
explanation: Standard formula: Z = I/y_max = (πd⁴/64)/(d/2) = πd³/32.

q: Centrifugal force acts at a curve
explanation: Centrifugal force is the outward pseudo-force acting away from the center of curvature.

q: Centrifugal force is given by
explanation: Centrifugal acceleration/specific force = v²/R (per unit mass form used in this option set).

q: Centrifugal force acts away from the center of the path while centripetal force
options: acts away from the center of path
acts towards the centre of path
explanation: As per the answer key for this set.

q: The shear force in a concrete beam is assumed to act
options: on a plane normal to the longitudinal axis
explanation: Transverse shear force acts perpendicular to the beam's longitudinal axis.

q: The shear force on a beam is proportional to
explanation: Shear force at a section equals the algebraic sum of all transverse forces on one side of that section.

q: Rate of change of bending moment is equal to
explanation: dM/dx = V — the fundamental beam relation between bending moment and shear force.

q: The rate of change of shear force is called
explanation: dV/dx = -w — the rate of change of shear force equals (negative) load intensity.

q: The amount of shear force at the maximum bending moment is
explanation: Since dM/dx = V, bending moment is maximum where shear force is zero (i.e. minimum).

q: In case of a simply supported beam subjected to UDL the maximum shear force occurs at a point
explanation: For UDL on a simply supported beam, shear force is maximum at the supports and zero at mid-span.

q: Shear force diagram for a cantilever carrying a UDL over its whole length is
explanation: SF varies linearly from zero at the free end to wL at the fixed end — a triangle.

q: The difference in ordinate of the shear force between any two sections is equal to the area under
options: shear curve between these two sections
load curve between these two sections
bending moment curve between these two sections
load curve between these two sections plus concentrated load applied between the sections
explanation: ΔV between two sections = area under the load intensity diagram between them.

q: In an I section almost all the shear force is taken by
explanation: The web carries the vast majority (~90%+) of the transverse shear force in an I-section.

q: A Prismatic bar when subjected to pure bending assumes the shape of
explanation: Under pure (constant) bending moment, a prismatic bar bends into a circular arc of constant curvature.

q: If a constant section is subjected to a uniform/pure bending moment throughout, its length bends to
explanation: Constant bending moment produces constant curvature — hence a circular arc.

q: A cable subjected to U.D.L. over its entire span assumes a shape of
explanation: A cable under uniformly distributed load (per horizontal length) hangs in a parabolic shape.

q: The shear flow in a section can be defined as
options: total shear stress at a point
explanation: Shear flow q = τ·t is related to the shear stress at a point in a thin-walled section.

q: The algebraic sum of the shear flow of a section in any direction must be equal to
explanation: Shear flow forms a self-balancing internal system, summing to zero around a closed section.

q: The shear center may be defined as
options: the point through which the resultant of the shear stress passes
the point about which the moment of shear flow of section is zero
the shear force in that direction
explanation: The shear center is the point of application of transverse load through which no twisting occurs — the resultant shear stress passes through it.

q: The shear center in the case of a T-beam section is
options: at the C.G. of the section
at the neutral axis of the section
on the C.G. horizontal plane and away from C.G. within the leg projections
explanation: For a T-section, the shear center coincides with the centroid due to its axis of symmetry.

q: The shear force and bending moment are related by
explanation: The fundamental beam relation: shear force = rate of change of bending moment, V = dM/dx.

q: A shear force diagram of a simply supported beam shows constant shear force throughout the span. It is subjected to
options: two concentrated loads spaced at points
explanation: A pure applied couple (no other transverse loads) produces a constant shear force with a jump in the moment diagram, but constant SF throughout.

q: The shear force on a beam and the displacement are related by
explanation: As per the answer key; the standard beam relation is V = EI·d³y/dx³ (third derivative of deflection).

q: The maximum number of transverse shear forces possible at one end of an element of a plane frame are
explanation: At each joint of a plane frame element, up to two transverse shear components can exist (in-plane, general loading).

q: The maximum number of transverse shear forces possible at one end of an element of a plane truss are
explanation: Truss members carry only axial force (two-force members) — no transverse shear develops at the ends.

q: Find the maximum BM induced in a simply supported beam if the beam is subjected to a point load of 4 KN at the centre of beam and span of the beam is 4 m
In a simply supported beam subjected to a point load at centre, the maximum bending moment occurs at
explanation: For a central point load on a simply supported beam, max BM occurs directly under the load, at mid-span.
